messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 76
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Ship Captain
  trauma_type: Police violence
  pcl5: 52

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Overworking: I throw myself into work or tasks to keep my mind occupied, Rumination: Meaning: go over and over why the event happened to me, Past Dwelling: I dwell on how I used to be before the event
  Memory: Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed., Photographic Recall: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind., Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

At 76, Ingrid Sorensen had spent most of her adult life on the water. A widowed ship captain on the Great Lakes, she was used to being the calmest person on deck, the one who could read weather, machinery, and men in a glance. The event that undid that certainty happened onshore after a late docking, when a police stop outside the port escalated with bewildering speed. She still describes the light first: the hard blue-red wash across wet pavement, the glare catching in the side mirror, the officer’s hand already on his weapon before she had fully stepped from the truck. She remembers being shoved against the vehicle, her cheek pressed to cold metal, hearing someone shout over her that she was “not complying” while her arms were forced behind her. What has stayed with her is not a blurred outline but a series of fixed images with punishing clarity: the reflection of the cruiser lights in a puddle, the seam in the officer’s glove, the grit on the hood inches from her eyes. When the memory comes, it does not feel like a story from the past. It arrives as if she is there again, her body braced, breath caught, waiting for the next blow.

In the weeks after, Ingrid found there was no gradual softening of the scene. The memory remained vivid, almost photographic, and at odd moments she would feel herself pulled back into it so completely that the dockyard or galley around her briefly disappeared. A flash of police lights near the harbor, the metallic slam of a truck door, even the pattern of reflected light on wet concrete could bring up those frozen frames with such immediacy that she felt ambushed by her own mind. She had come to dread idle moments because they left room for the pictures to break through. To keep that from happening, she began filling every hour she could. She stayed on the vessel longer than necessary after runs, volunteered for extra paperwork, reorganized inventory no one had asked her to touch, and kept herself moving through maintenance lists she once would have delegated. If she was exhausted enough, she thought, there might be less room for the images.

That strategy gradually became the structure of her days. At the port office she took on tasks younger captains shrugged off, remaining long after the crew had gone home, checking manifests repeatedly and scrubbing at small logistical problems as if precision could quiet her mind. When work finally could not be stretched any further, her thoughts turned inward and began circling. She went over and over why this had happened to her, a woman with decades of command experience and no history of trouble, searching for some explanation that would make the assault feel less arbitrary. Just as often she found herself dwelling on who she had been before that night—steady, respected, unflinching—and measuring that earlier self against the woman who now scanned every roadside stop and worked until her hands shook with fatigue.

Yet the more she lived this way, the less the memory loosened. Long hours and constant tasks did not file the event away; they seemed to sharpen it. After days of driving herself without pause, the images would break through with startling crispness the moment she slowed down, as if everything she had been holding off surged forward at once. Ruminating on why it happened only fixed her attention more tightly on the details she could not solve, and dwelling on the person she used to be made the scene of being pinned to the truck feel even more brutal and definitive. By now she could summon, unwillingly, exact visual fragments she wished she could forget: the angle of the flashlight beam, the officer’s stance, the smeared red-blue color over the dockside asphalt. What frightened her most was how present it still felt. Even knowing she was back on her ship, she could suddenly feel the same helpless jolt in her body, as if time had folded and she was once again an old woman being handled like a threat.

The pattern has begun to cost her in ways she cannot dismiss as simple grit. Crew members have noticed that Captain Sorensen no longer leaves tasks unfinished or hands work off easily; she hovers, rechecks, and stays aboard so late that others avoid raising concerns with her at the end of a shift. She knows she is using the ship to keep her mind occupied, but she also knows the relief is thin and temporary. What finally brought her to seek help was a recent evening at the harbor when police lights flashed at the far end of the dock. She froze with a coil of rope in her hands, and for a few seconds the pavement, the shouting, and the pressure against her arms were not memories but something she was living through again. Later, alone in her cabin, she worked until nearly dawn and then lay awake asking why this had happened and whether the capable woman she used to be was gone for good. She comes to treatment wanting, more than anything, to stop being dragged back into that night, and fearing that if she ever stops pushing herself, the memory will take over completely.
